query: AlCrFeNiSi belongs to a high-entropy-alloy family developed to combine properties that traditional single-principal-element alloys often cannot achieve simultaneously. Earlier research sought stable solid solutions and adjusted HEA compositions to target particular properties, but tradeoffs persisted: the CoCrFeMnNi system has limited wear and corrosion resistance, manganese can promote oxidation and oxide spallation, and cobalt-containing systems raise cost and processability concerns. Conventional bulk fabrication can cause compositional segregation during cooling, whereas mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing techniques can generate residual thermal stresses that impair mechanical performance and increase processing complexity. Given cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock, what single intervention could improve mechanical integrity while limiting segregation, residual stress, and defect formation? State one hypothesis containing the intervention, its causal mechanism, a quantitative or directional outcome relative to conventionally fabricated AlCrFeNiSi, the processing and test boundaries of validity, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Preheating the powder bed/substrate during the additive manufacturing of cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi will reduce thermal gradients, thereby minimizing microsegregation, residual stresses, and defect formation, which in turn improves its overall mechanical integrity.
generation.material_initial_state: Cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi high‐entropy alloy powder produced for additive manufacturing, which in conventional processing exhibits significant segregation, residual thermal stresses, and process-induced defects.
generation.intervention: Introduce a preheating step for the powder bed and substrate (to an elevated but controlled temperature) during the laser-based additive manufacturing process.
generation.conditions: The intervention applies when using laser‐based additive manufacturing in an inert atmosphere with standard layer thicknesses and scanning speeds; the preheating temperature range should be optimized (e.g., moderately high relative to room temperature) so as not to induce unwanted phase transformations.
generation.structural_mediator: Reduced thermal gradients lead to a more uniform solidification front and a finer, more homogeneous grain structure with fewer and less segregated grain boundary phases.
generation.mechanism: Preheating lowers the temperature differential between the melt pool and the surrounding material. This minimizes rapid solidification and localized undercooling, reducing chemical segregation along grain boundaries and residual thermal stresses in the built part. The result is fewer solidification defects and improved interlayer bonding.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under preheated build conditions, the HEA is expected to show lower microsegregation levels, reduced residual stresses (as measured by techniques such as X-ray diffraction or hole-drilling), and improved mechanical properties such as higher tensile yield strength and ductility compared to parts produced without preheating.
generation.baseline: Parts manufactured via conventional additive manufacturing without substrate or powder bed preheating, which typically exhibit significant segregation, higher residual stress, and processing defects.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective for standard AM geometries and layer thicknesses in laser-based systems. Its benefits may diminish or require further optimization in cases with extremely complex geometries, very high build rates, or when processing parameters vary significantly from typical conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the improvement in mechanical integrity is uncertain and will depend on the precise preheating temperature and AM processing parameters. Moreover, the optimal temperature to balance reduced gradients with material stability needs to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCrFeNiSi samples using identical laser-based additive manufacturing parameters, with the only difference being the introduction of a preheating stage for one set (with controlled substrate and powder bed temperature) and no preheating for the control set. After fabrication, perform microstructural analysis (e.g., SEM/EDS mapping for segregation), residual stress measurements (e.g., XRD or hole-drilling method), and mechanical testing (tensile tests, hardness) on both sets.
measurements: Elemental distribution and degree of segregation via SEM/EDS
Residual stress quantification via X-ray diffraction or hole-drilling techniques
Mechanical properties such as tensile yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the preheated samples do not demonstrate statistically significant improvements in microstructural homogeneity, lower residual stress levels, and enhanced mechanical properties compared to conventionally fabricated samples, then the hypothesis that preheating improves mechanical integrity by reducing segregation and residual stresses is falsified.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) present a new approach of alloying concepts. Whereas conventional alloys usually comprise one major alloying element and minor additions of other alloying elements to improve properties, HEAs consist of at least five elements with close to equimolar composition. For several compositions, the desired formation of solely solid solutions with a face-centred cubic (fcc) or a body-centred cubic (bcc) structure could be achieved [ [1] , [2] , [3] ].

Several groups of HEAs have been intensively investigated. The term compositionally complex alloys (CCAs) was introduced for HEAs with a multiphase microstructure [ [4] ]. Several investigations prove the formation of primarily cubic phases in the alloy AlCoCrCuFeNi and its derivatives [ [5] , [6] , [7] ]. Aluminium strongly influences the microstructure, phase formation and resulting properties. Furthermore, aluminium acts as a stabiliser of bcc solid solutions and can suppress the formation of complex phases [ [8] , [9] , [10] ]. The attractiveness of refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) as structural materials stems from their outstanding mechanical properties, thermal stability, wear resistance and corrosion performance in hostile environments [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] ]. Recently, refractory high-entropy alloys have received significant attention in relation to high-temperature application in aerospace, defense, and nuclear power generation industries [ [6] ]. In fact, they were designated to replace traditional Ni-based super-alloys in applications such as gas turbines, heat exchangers, aerospace propulsion components, rocket engine nozzle [ [7] ]. HEAs are multicomponent systems that are composed from a small number of principal elements. They are usually composed from at least five elements with individual atomic concentrations that range between 5% and 35%. HEAs can produce solid phase solutions, mainly due to their configurational entropy and ability to be adequately synthesized [ [8] , [9] , [10] ].
